title: Comprehensive MR Fingerprinting for Infants and Young Children at Risk for Developmental Delays
text:
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is an important tool for imaging babies and monitoring brain development
that influences long-term health outcomes. This project is to develop a novel quantitative MR scan called MR
Fingerprinting tailored for baby imaging and use this scan to assess babies with opioid exposure. The goal is to
use this technique to identify babies with high risk for developmental delays who may benefit from early
intervention.

title: 2/1 - Mongolian Center for Environmental & Occupational Health - Mongolia
text: In the United States, air pollution from wildfires, industry, and urban traffic drives significant respiratory disease, but studying these effects domestically is limited by relatively lower pollutant levels and ethical constraints. This project leverages Mongolia’s extreme air pollution as a natural experimental model to investigate how pollutant mixtures cause respiratory harm, integrating epidemiological studies with cell-based toxicology (U01). Training Mongolian scholars (U2R) builds sustainable expertise for U.S.-Mongolia partnerships, generating actionable insights to protect the health of Americans living in polluted regions.

title: Biostatistics/Bioinformatics Core
text:
Successful completion of the scientific objectives of the Mayo/UMN Prostate SPORE requires high-quality
biostatistics and bioinformatics support to maintain state-of-the-art data analysis and management for each
SPORE Project and the CEP/DRP Programs. The Biostatistics/Bioinformatics Core (Core C) will serve as a
centralized resource to meet the study design and data analysis needs of the SPORE Projects and Programs
by: (1) supporting the design, implementation, analysis, integration and dissemination of results, (2) devising a
comprehensive plan to manage, deposit and store statistical/informatics data, and (3) facilitating interactions
among the Projects and Programs, including pan-SPORE secondary analyses. By centralizing these functions
under a common core, we will ensure that all Projects and Programs within the SPORE benefit from consistent,
high-quality, biostatistical and bioinformatics support.

title: Post-transcriptional Regulatory Networks
text:
This project combines large-scale, biochemical assays with artificial intelligence techniques to determine the
vocabulary of the instructions used by our cells to determine which genes are active under which conditions.
Discovering the words (called motifs) of this vocabulary will help scientists to understand which mutations
change these instructions and how these changes lead to cancer and other human diseases. As new motifs
are uncovered, the sequences of human messenger RNAs will be scanned to try to assign meaning to the
motif vocabulary.

title: Optimized clinical dermal Open Flow Microperfusion study design to demonstrate bioequivalence based on cutaneous pharmacokinetics
text:
Accessibility and affordability of topically applied drug products (TADPs) is compromised by an
extraordinary price increase during the last decade due to a low number of approved generic TADPs.
Project beOFM will expand the scientific basis for cutaneous bioequivalence assessment with dermal
continuous sampling techniques, and will thus help policy makers to evaluate the use of cutaneous
bioequivalence studies instead of clinical endpoint studies for generic TADP approval. This will lower the
barrier for generic TADP development, increase the number of generic TADP approvals and will thus help
to increase accessibility and affordability of TADPs.
1

title: FoxO transcription factors in joint aging and osteoarthritis pathogenesis
text:
This study is based on our recent findings that the expression of FoxO transcription factors is
suppressed in articular cartilage from aged and osteoarthritis-affected human and mouse joints. The
proposed research will investigate the role of FoxO in joint homeostasis, consequences of FoxO
suppression in joint aging and osteoarthritis pathogenesis and determine potential therapeutic
benefits of increasing FoxO expression. The findings from this work have potential to lead to a
paradigm shift in the understanding of the impact of joint aging on osteoarthritis pathogenesis and
lead to new approaches to prevention and treatment.
!

title: Sex Differences in HIV-1 Reservoir- a Multi-omic Approach to Identify Mechanisms of Reservoir Decay
text:
HIV-1 infection cannot be cured in most people due to the persistence of a latent reservoir, despite long-term
suppressive antiretroviral therapy (ART), and therefore, it is crucial to understand the dynamics of the HIV-1
reservoir and the determinants of its persistence, as emerging evidence has demonstrated that after 10-20
years of suppressive ART, the reservoir may plateau or even increase in some individuals. I hypothesize that
aging and biological sex are associated with HIV-1 proviral dynamics through hormonal changes and
inflammation. I will longitudinally characterize HIV-1 proviral levels using IPDA and correlate demographics,
menopausal status in women, endogenous hormone levels, soluble immunological markers, and peripheral
blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) single-cell sequencing data to holistically understand the aging, sex,
endocrinological, and immunological correlates of HIV-1 proviral dynamics.

title: Dissection of the Molecular Basis of Pleiotropy Between GnRH Neuronal Development and Cranial Suture Fusion
text:
Pleiotropy is a poorly understood phenomenon in human genetic disorders wherein defects in a single gene
results in multiple seemingly unrelated clinical conditions. In this proposal, the investigators will identity and
characterize human genes that interconnect disorders of reproduction and craniofacial development. Using
human studies and zebrafish models, this study will help understand the extent of genetic pleiotropy, the reasons
behind the pleiotropy of these genes and its effects on overall human health.

title: 3/3 Akili: Phenotypic and genetic characterization of ADHD in Kenya and South Africa
text: Genetic research into attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) lags in terms of both sample size and consideration of phenotypic heterogeneity. The Akili project will address both of these critical gaps, phenotypically and genetically characterizing 4,000 children with ADHD and 2,000 age- and ancestry-matched controls in Kenya and South Africa. Akili will unite genetic sequencing with deep clinical phenotyping expertise to improve biological understanding of ADHD, a common and impactful diagnosis for families in the United States; and will also introduce genomic data currently missing from reference databases, directly advancing genetic diagnostic accuracy and precision medicine for all U.S. demographic groups.

title: Long noncoding RNA-mediated regulation of T-cell alloimmunity
text:
Acute graft-versus-host disease (aGVHD) is a major complication of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell
transplantation, and improved therapies for aGVHD are needed. To develop potential new targets for
improving aGVHD, our group recently identified a novel T cell-enriched long noncoding RNA, LINC00402, that
uniquely promotes allogeneic T-cell proliferation. We now seek to determine LINC00402’s function and
molecular mechanism in both mice and humans.

title: Cardiovascular regeneration and pioneer factors
text:
Cardiovascular disease is common and contributes to the morbidity and mortality of our patients. The
longterm goal and the clinical significance of this proposal are to define the initial factors that govern the
stem cell/progenitors to promote the formation of new vessels in response to injury or disease. The results
from these studies will serve as an important platform for therapeutic initiatives focused on cardiovascular
disease.

title: Interpretable Real-Time Surgical Skill Assessment Via Optical Neuroimaging
text:
Surgical skill assessment via functional near infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) shows great promise for providing
online feedback on surgical task performance, however, the extensive post-hoc processing which is standard
in the field of fNIRS precludes its use in many online applications. To resolve this, we propose a deep learning-
enabled, task-agnostic fNIRS denoising pipeline, trained and validated on experimental and/or synthetic data
from a novel synthetic data generator which will be developed using amortized simulation-based inference.
Finally, through deep learning, we will predict the FLS score, a widely used surgical skill performance metric,
based on the fNIRS neural signatures, for online surgical skill assessment, with explainable AI technique
implementation for additional interpretability of predicted scores.

title: Imaging Core D
text: PROJECT SUMMARY - IMAGING CORE Imaging Core D of the Perimenopause Program Project is a centralized resource that enables high-throughput, standardized small animal PET and MRI acquisition, processing, and both mouse and human neuroimaging analyses to investigate imaging-derived signatures of menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) in order to understand why MHT timing and formulation confer differential AD risk profiles. Its primary mission is to generate and analyze multimodal neuroimaging data to characterize how menopause-related metabolic disruption initiates and propagates neurodegeneration and the potential for MHT mediated rescue. To this end, Imaging Core D will employ a hybrid small-animal PET/MRI platform with radiotracers targeting glucose metabolism (FDG) coupled with high-resolution MRI for structural, diffusion, susceptibility, and relaxometry imaging. All small animal imaging data will be collected under harmonized protocols and stored in a centralized BIDS- compliant format with rich metadata to ensure reproducibility and facilitate cross-project integration. Preprocessing pipelines include denoising, artifact correction, bias correction, and spatial normalization to project-specific mouse brain templates. Data will be transformed into both voxel-wise and region-based maps, which are used to extract treatment-related patterns (TRPs) using advanced dimensionality reduction approaches such as PCA and non-negative matrix factorization. To maximize translational potential, human structural and diffusion weighted imaging data will undergo similar storage, preprocessing, and spatial mapping to link MHT outcomes in patients with the multimodal imaging obtained in the mice. These TRPs quantify spatial metabolic and structural deviations and will be used to compare treatment and vehicle groups, assess bioenergetic rescue, and link imaging signatures to molecular and behavioral outcomes. Region-based profiling will facilitate hierarchical Bayesian modeling of group differences, metabolic connectivity analyses, and multimodal correlations with gene expression and histology data aligned to the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas. The Imaging Core is foundational to the Perimenopause Program’s ability to identify biomarkers and mechanistic targets of MHT-mediated AD risk, supporting both discovery science and translational innovation.

title: Tanzania AIDS Malignancies Training and Research Program (TAMTRP)
text: Cancers are a major cause of death globally among people living with HIV, and the disproportionately high burden of oncogenic virus infection-associated malignancies in Tanzania provides a unique scientific opportunity to generate insights that can improve cancer prevention, early detection, and treatment for HIV-infected-at-risk populations in the U.S. The Tanzania AIDS Malignancies Training and Research Program (TAMTRP) addresses critical gaps in cancer research capacity at the Ocean Road Cancer Institute (ORCI) in Dar es Salaam by training Tanzanian fellows, researchers, and practitioners, which facilitates leveraging of Tanzania’s distinct epidemiology, limited prior genomic characterization, and high case volume of virally driven cancers that cannot be replicated in U.S.-only settings. Through this work, TAMTRP will strengthen clinical, public health, cancer biology, and genomics/bioinformatics research across both partner institutions, enhance collaborations for the U.S. cancer researchers, and thereby produce knowledge and workforce capacity that translate into improved clinical care and reduced cancer disparities in both Tanzania and the U.S.

title: Project 1: Endothelial cell programs for coronary artery disease
text: Project 1 Coronary artery disease (CAD) remains the leading cause of death throughout the world despite therapies targeting leading risk factors, calling for the rapid development of new treatments. One approach is to use human genetic association studies to identify medically targetable pathways. However, finding disease-causing genes has been a slow endeavor because it requires testing one gene at a time and there are over 300 CAD loci. Our lab recently demonstrated that a new technology called Perturb-seq can dramatically increase this discovery pipeline because it can functionally characterize all 300 CAD loci in one experiment by identifying convergence of risk pathways. When we performed this assay in primary human endothelial cells (ECs), we discovered that 41 CAD risk loci converge onto a small number of common pathways that could promote disease risk. The major disease-associated pathway we identified contained several genes previously associated with Cerebral Cavernous Malformations (CCM), a rare neurovascular disease. Common variants in the CCM-signaling pathway were consistently protective for CAD risk, despite established pathogenic roles for these genes for neurovascular disease. We showed that two CAD-associated genes—CCM2 and TLNRD1—interact in the CCM complex and regulate many other CAD risk genes and the endothelial shear stress response. Given this success, Project 1 will use our recently developed in vivo Perturb-seq capabilities to rapidly map out disease mechanisms of the CCM pathway in the whole organism and identify CAD gene programs active in diseased arteries. Specifically, we need to understand why mutations in the CCM-signaling pathway are pathogenic for cerebrovascular disease, but protective for CAD. Our experiments will address the central hypothesis that the CCM signaling pathway is a major determinant of CAD risk, with context-dependent effects on ECs that depend on the stage of atherosclerosis, dosage/degree of gene inhibition, and EC subtypes from vascular beds in different organs. Applying new innovations for in vivo Perturb-seq developed by our Scientific Cores, the Aims of Project 1 are to 1) determine context-dependent effects of 250 genes in 3 stages of murine atherosclerosis; 2) characterize the effects of EC-specific TLNRD1 knockout on atherosclerosis, vascular development, arteriogenesis, and angiogenesis; and 3) identify the organotypic effects of CCM2/TLNRD1 knockdown in brain, lung, and aortic ECs. Our study will be highly synergistic with the other Projects in the Program, enabling comparison of causal CAD programs between ECs and smooth muscle cells (with Project 2), and comparisons of the functions of EC genes and programs between two distinct diseases (CAD vs. pulmonary arterial hypertension with Project 3). Through integration across all 3 Projects, we will address the central goal of the Program to identify cell-type specific effects of causal genes in multiple vascular cell types and prioritize the pathways with the greatest translational relevance for therapy and prevention.

title: Environmental and Developmental Regulation of Primordial Germ Cell Proliferation in the C. Elegans Larval Gonad
text:
Primordial germ cells (PGCs) are the founders of the germline, dividing to produce the sperm and egg required
to sustain life in sexually reproducing animals. PGCs rely on their local microenvironment called the niche to
integrate environmental and developmental cues to signal for PGC division. This proposal uses C. elegans
larval niche signaling to identify mechanisms controlling the transition from PGC quiescence to proliferation,
with greater implications applied to human infertility and germline tumors.

title: Role and Mechanisms of VAV1 alterations in Peripheral T-cell Lymphomas
text:
This project aims to analyze the role of VAV1-MYO1F a recurrent activating genetic alteration driving activation
of the guanine nucleotide exchange factor VAV1 in Peripheral T-cell Lymphomas (PTCL). To dissect the role of
the recurrent VAV1-MYO1F fusion, we will use a newly developed genetically engineered mouse model of
lymphoma and characterize these tumors using a combination of molecular pathology and genomic profiling
tools. Elucidation of the specific mechanisms mediating the oncogenic effects of VAV1-MYO1F will provide
important novel insight on the pathogenesis of peripheral T-cell lymphomas and point to novel targets to be
tested in experimental therapeutics.

title: Elucidating the role of Scribble in angiogenic symmetry breaking and adherens junction remodeling
text:
Angiogenesis is crucial for tissue homeostasis and growth, yet it remains unclear how angiogenesis is
spatially and temporally regulated to drive proper neovascularization therapeutically in settings such as tissue
ischemia, or to block vascularization of tumors. This study will use innovative tissue-engineered human
microvessels and sophisticated molecular and imaging approaches to deepen our understanding of endothelial
control systems that enable angiogenesis, and inform future efforts towards development of new therapeutic
interventions for driving or blocking tissue vascularization.

title: Developing a Selective PROTAC of Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase for Treatment of ALK+ NSCLC
text: The American Cancer Society estimates that 238,000 Americans will be diagnosed with lung cancer in 2023 and over 127,000 Americans will die of lung cancer complications. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for the vast majority (~82%) of all lung cancer diagnoses and can be caused by a number of distinct mechanisms. One such mechanism is an inversion of part of Chromosome 2p that leads to the fusion of the tyrosine kinase domain of the Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase (ALK) gene with coiled-coil domain of echinoderm microtubule-associated protein-like 4 gene (EML4), leading to a soluble, dimerized, constitutively active tyrosine kinase. While a series of competitive ALK inhibitors have been approved by the FDA in the last decade, spontaneous suppressor mutations in the ALK active site limit their efficacy, with median duration of response of 11 months. Rather than continue to develop ALK inhibitors, we have developed a series of proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) to induce the degradation of the EML4-ALK protein. These heterobifunctional PROTACs are small molecules that contain an EML4-ALK targeting motif, a flexible linker, and a ligand that recruits an E3 ubiquitin ligase. This complex induces the ubiquitination and subsequent proteasome-mediated degradation of the target protein. In cellular assays, we see that our early stage PROTACs induce degradation of transformed, NSCLC-causing EML4-ALK fusions, as well as EML4-ALK with suppressor mutations that block the efficacy of currently approved therapeutics. Importantly, we observe EML4-ALK degradation for concentrations at or lower than those used for current inhibitors. In the initial stages of this proposal, we will perform iterative synthesis and testing of additional PROTAC molecules to increase both their selectivity and effectiveness in in vitro and cellular studies. Once we have obtained the most promising candidates for further development, we will test them for a comprehensive set of pharmaceutical criteria including desirable ADME and safety pharmacology profile, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, in vivo efficacy, and oral bioavailability. PROTACs that meet such criteria will then be tested in clinically relevant xenograft ALK-positive NSCLC tumor models to evaluate in vivo efficacy and pharmacodynamics, as well as additional ADME and PK studies. This work will develop a first-in class, orally active ALK degrader that can be used for patients that have become resistant to first-line inhibitor treatment. In addition, ALK degraders have the potential to be used as a first-line treatment as well, since they have already shown efficacy in degrading non-resistant forms of EML4-ALK fusions.

title: Interrogation of Non-Canonical Roles of VGSCs in Neurodevelopmental Epilepsy
text:
Voltage-gated sodium channels (VGSCs) mediate action potential propagation and transduction
in neurons, however, recent work has shown that VGSCs serve additional functions in non-
excitable cell types and in the developing nervous system. The potential contribution of these
“non-canonical” functions of VGSCs to the development of neurodevelopmental conditions
remains unknown. This proposed work will use human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived
brain organoids and genome engineering to investigate the molecular mechanism underlying
non-canonical VGSC contributions to neurological development and disease.
